title: Collecting Ambition
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This essay explores why highly ambitious team members are both prized and rare, and what separates them from the moderately ambitious majority. Most people, it argues, have a contentment threshold — a point where they've achieved enough and shift their energy toward other pursuits — while a rarer group never reaches that ceiling because their ambition is tied directly to self-esteem rather than external rewards. The piece notes that highly ambitious people can sometimes act in their own self-interest, but leaders still actively seek them out because they're disproportionately responsible for driving teams toward extraordinary outcomes. It closes by framing this kind of relentless achiever as a scarce, hard-to-manufacture asset.
points: Leaders prize ambitious team members because achieving extraordinary goals depends heavily on them.
Most people have a contentment threshold beyond which their drive to achieve levels off.
A rare group of people never hit that threshold because their ambition is tied to self-esteem, not just rewards.
For that rare group, achievement itself functions almost like a narcotic that keeps driving them.
Because such people are hard to find and even harder to manufacture, good leaders are always hunting for them.
quotes: The drive to achieve prized outcomes is an intangible that leaders can’t collect enough of.
Most team members are relatively ambitious—up to a point. The majority have a threshold or contentment point where they no longer need to attain more.
But a rare group of people never reach this point or threshold no matter how much they achieve or get compensated.
Their ambition is directly tied to their self-esteem, and they seem to feel even better about themselves with every successive achievement.
Money and other incentives they gather along the way represent a score regarding this satisfaction and usually little more. Achievement becomes the narcotic that drives their lives.
